_comment: MSSQL provider -- feature 11 (OWNER-DECISIONS.md Batch 5; feature doc
011-mssql-provider.md MSSQL-DEC-01 + MSSQL-DEC-02).
SQL Server is a first-class provider in all four frameworks. Its adapter papers
over three T-SQL facts: it has no RETURNING, its pagination syntax differs, and
the INSERT + last-id probe run in separate scopes. This fixture pins the
write-path + parameter behaviours a caller depends on, against a REAL SQL Server
:1433 (sa -> tina4_test), no mocks. Under TINA4_REQUIRE_SERVICES a skip here is
a hard FAILURE.
MSSQL-DEC-01 (safe parameter handling): the audit found two unsafe param paths.
* Ruby hand-interpolates params and its `else param.to_s` fell through to a
BAREWORD for any unrecognised type (a Symbol became `VALUES (foo)` -> an
invalid / injected statement). It now emits ASCII-8BIT bytes as a `0x`
varbinary literal and RAISES ArgumentError on a genuinely unbindable type --
never a bareword. Witnessed Ruby-only by `an unbindable parameter raises
instead of a bareword` (revert -> RED).
* Node inferred the TDS param type from the JS type (NVarChar default, else
Int/Float/Bit/DateTime) with NO Buffer branch, so a Buffer bound as NVarChar
and corrupted binary writes. It now maps a Buffer -> VarBinary (checked
first). Witnessed by the four-way binary case (revert -> RED in Node).
The FOUR-WAY observable is `a binary parameter round trips intact`: Python's
pymssql binds bytes natively; Node binds VarBinary; PHP and Ruby inline a `0x`
literal because FreeTDS (pdo_dblib / tiny_tds) CANNOT carry raw binary through
a `?` bind -- MEASURED on the lab: a NUL byte breaks the TDS stream (even
PDO::PARAM_LOB fails), while a `0x` literal round-trips byte-for-byte. A
companion `a text parameter round trips intact` guards that the binary
detection never mis-routes ordinary UTF-8 text through the 0x path.
MSSQL-DEC-02 (real-PK RETURNING): SQL Server has no RETURNING, so the PYTHON
adapter strips it and re-selects the inserted row. It fetched by a HARDCODED
`id` column (`... WHERE id = %s`), so a table whose PK is NOT named `id` raised
'Invalid column name id'. Python now re-selects by the table's REAL primary key
(introspected, bracket-quoted with embedded `]` escaped, cached) -- the same
defect + fix feature 10 applied to mysql.py, shared with firebird.py.
IMPORTANT SCOPE (verified against all four live adapters): the RETURNING *record*
emulation exists ONLY in the Python adapter. PHP/Ruby/Node do NOT emulate MSSQL
RETURNING; they surface the generated key through SCOPE_IDENTITY, which is tied
to the IDENTITY column and is therefore COLUMN-NAME-INDEPENDENT -- so a non-`id`-
PK insert already returns the correct generated last-id in all four (invariant
1). Per the owner governance rule (fix the broken one, do NOT mirror a mechanism
the others do not need), the hardcoded-`id` fix is Python-adapter-local; the
observable contract is proven four-way. The Python-only `returning_*` tests are
the direct mutation witness (revert -> 'Invalid column name id' RED).
MSSQL-DEC-02 (one pagination strategy): the MSSQL pagination strategy DIVERGED --
Python/PHP/Ruby append OFFSET/FETCH (the modern standard, with an injected
`ORDER BY (SELECT NULL)` when none is present), while NODE branched to `TOP n`
for the first page (skip 0) and OFFSET/FETCH only for a non-zero skip. All four
now use the ONE strategy -- OFFSET/FETCH -- so `fetchAsync` no longer emits TOP
for a page-one read (TOP 0 remains only for the degenerate limit=0 = zero-rows
case OFFSET/FETCH cannot express). Proven four-way by the offset window: a
TOP-only strategy that ignores the offset returns the FIRST page for a later-
page request. ZERO new runtime dependencies in any framework.
Env contract (the canonical TINA4_TEST_MSSQL_* convention, identical to the
other live MSSQL tests): TINA4_TEST_MSSQL_HOST / _PORT / _USERNAME / _PASSWORD /
_DB, defaulting to 127.0.0.1:1433 sa / TinaSQL123!Secure -> tina4_test. On the
lab only the pdo_dblib / FreeTDS PHP leg runs (ext-sqlsrv is unverified there);
the 0x-literal binary fix is standard T-SQL and applies to BOTH PHP backends.
feature: 11 - MSSQL provider (MSSQL-DEC-01 safe parameter handling - Ruby unknown-type bareword, Node Buffer->VarBinary, four-way binary round-trip; MSSQL-DEC-02 real-PK RETURNING emulation Python-local with a non-`id`-PK regression proven four-way, and ONE OFFSET/FETCH pagination strategy across all four), against a real SQL Server

invariants.rule: On a real SQL Server, db.insert() into a table whose PRIMARY KEY is NOT named `id` returns a DatabaseResult whose last_id is the generated IDENTITY key (surfaced via the column-independent SCOPE_IDENTITY, never a hardcoded-`id` fetch) and whose affected_rows is 1; a second insert returns the NEXT generated id, never a stale earlier one; the row is durably keyed by the real primary key, read back on a SECOND fresh connection. Identical in all four (Python Database.insert -> MSSQLAdapter; PHP Database::insert -> MSSQLAdapter; Ruby Database#insert -> MssqlDriver; Node Database.insert -> MssqlAdapter).
invariants.why: MSSQL-RETURNING-ID: the user-observable symptom of the hardcoded-`id` emulation was 'an insert into a table whose PK is NOT `id` returns the wrong / no last-id'. This pins the correct observable -- the generated key comes back for a non-`id` PK -- against a real IDENTITY table with a non-`id` PK. It is green four-way because SCOPE_IDENTITY() is tied to the IDENTITY column, not to a column named `id`; it is the regression lock that guards against ever deriving the last-id from a hardcoded-`id` fetch. The Python adapter's RETURNING *record* emulation (the actual defect site) is additionally mutation-witnessed by the Python suite's `returning_*` tests. No mocks.
cases: a non id primary key insert returns the generated last id
a second non id primary key insert returns the next generated id
a non id primary key insert reports affected rows of one

invariants.rule: On a real SQL Server, a binary parameter (Python bytes, PHP/Ruby a raw-byte string, Node a Buffer) written through the public write path round-trips byte-for-byte into a VARBINARY column, read back on a SECOND fresh connection: Node binds it as TDS VarBinary; Python's pymssql binds bytes natively; PHP and Ruby inline it as a `0x` varbinary literal (FreeTDS cannot bind raw binary through a `?` placeholder). An ordinary UTF-8 text parameter still round-trips intact on the bound / quoted path, with correct quote-escaping, and is never mis-routed through the binary path. Identical observable in all four.
invariants.why: MSSQL-BUFFER-NODE + MSSQL-INTERP-RUBY: a Buffer used to bind as NVarChar in Node (a text encoding applied to bytes -> corruption), and Ruby's hand-rolled interpolator emitted a bareword for an unrecognised type. Binary is the concrete 'unusual-typed param' MSSQL-DEC-01 centres on; proven four-way against a real VARBINARY column with a payload that carries a NUL byte and high bytes -- exactly what a text bind / quoted string corrupts. MEASURED on the lab: pdo_dblib CANNOT bind that payload through `?` (even PDO::PARAM_LOB fails), a `0x` literal round-trips. Mutation-proved: revert Node Buffer->VarBinary -> the binary case RED in Node; revert Ruby's binary branch -> RED in Ruby. The Ruby unknown-type BAREWORD fix is additionally mutation-witnessed Ruby-only by the suite's `an unbindable parameter raises instead of a bareword` test (a Symbol raises ArgumentError instead of splicing a bareword). No mocks.
cases: a binary parameter round trips intact
a text parameter round trips intact

invariants.rule: On a real SQL Server, a paginated read db.fetch(sql, params, limit, offset) with an explicit ORDER BY returns the correct WINDOW via OFFSET ... ROWS FETCH NEXT ... ROWS ONLY -- the FIRST page (limit 2, offset 0 -> rows 1,2) and a LATER page (limit 2, offset 2 -> rows 3,4) each return exactly their window. All four frameworks use the ONE OFFSET/FETCH strategy; Node no longer branches to `TOP n` for the first page. Identical in all four.
invariants.why: MSSQL-PAGINATION-DIVERGE: Python/PHP/Ruby appended OFFSET/FETCH while Node used `TOP n` for skip 0 (same window, divergent SQL, and the `^SELECT` regex could not prefix a CTE / leading-comment SELECT). Converging on OFFSET/FETCH removes the divergence with zero new deps. Proven behaviourally by the offset window on a real 5-row table: a TOP-only strategy that ignores the offset returns the FIRST page [1,2] for a later-page (offset 2) request, so the case is a real gate. Mutation-proved: force TOP / drop the offset -> 'a paginated query returns a later page window with offset' goes RED. No mocks.
cases: a paginated query returns the first page window
a paginated query returns a later page window with offset
